topic: A Public AI Whose Memory Is Shared Across All Users: Implications

key_points: Once several agents share one store, the memory cache becomes a multi-user data system and inherits the 'who may read what' question.
A retrieval-time policy filter authorizes the wrong unit: memory systems derive new records (summaries, personas, skills) that a filter has never seen, and revocation leaves derivatives behind.
Database precedent: application-side WHERE clauses lost to row-level security, and RLS itself needed PostgreSQL 15 security_invoker views because derived objects leaked around it.

Aug 2026 bracket: TencentDB Agent Memory 2.0 (Aug 3) shipped team memory with private-by-default ACLs; MAP-Graph (arXiv, Aug 11) argues authorization must be intrinsic to the memory graph so restrictions propagate through derivation.
Team memory breaks the single-user model: sales commissions, HR performance notes, support complaints must not cross principals.
A 'where user_id = current_user' clause inside agent code is a label, not a boundary — one misconfigured prompt or injection defeats it.
Three-tier design: private (owner only), team (group-scoped), global (org-wide, admin-write).
Conservative defaults: agent writes default to private; promotion to team/global needs review or a confidence check; classification runs before the write commits.
Audit every read/write in a separate append-only table; embeddings leak too (similarity probing reveals content).
Statelessness was an accidental security property: a malicious input died with the session. Persistent shared memory removes it.

Memory poisoning (OWASP prompt-injection given a longer life) survives session resets and travels into every later interaction; vectors include direct injection, RAG poisoning, embedding manipulation, and corrupted cross-session summaries.
Embeddings are not anonymization — inversion attacks reconstruct short high-value strings (names, emails). A vector store of regulated data is a regulated data store.
Regulatory pull in two directions: GDPR Art 17 erasure vs EU AI Act Art 12/19 logging (≥6 months, up to 10 years of technical documentation).
Control stack: write-path validation + provenance, read-path storage-layer isolation + authorization-before-return, lifecycle TTL/versioning + encryption.
Two layers people conflate: a memory engine (recall for one app) vs a governed brain (permissions, audit, provenance across a fleet).
Benchmark numbers for recall are not governance: LongMemEval — Zep 63.8%, Mem0 49.0%.
Give each agent a verifiable identity (ERC-8004) instead of one shared key, or per-agent permissions and a meaningful audit are impossible.

Permission-aware retrieval: check identity against each source's real permissions before returning anything; redact single fields rather than withholding documents; content-blind tamper-evident access log.
MCP turns memory into distributed, persistent, interoperable infrastructure — data now crosses tools, devices, and sessions without prompts or transparency.

Three breakages: opacity (users cannot track what the agent knows), consent (one prompt cascades into dozens of unseen service actions), data minimization (distributed memory makes auditing collection infeasible).
Encryption ends at the orchestration layer: to summarize or act, the agent must read plaintext, so the trust boundary moves to a layer with weak auditability.
Proposes interoperable memory dashboards, default retention limits for health/finance, memory-free modes, orchestration-layer data protection, and memory portability.
'Information soup': pooling diverse personal data into one unstructured store makes cross-context leaks structural, not a policy bug.
Reflection layers are a second leak vector: a user model that summarizes across partitions collapses the walls at the abstraction level even when raw memory is partitioned.
Provenance metadata (source, timestamp, interaction context) is the missing primitive; without it consent toggles are theater.
Documented exploits against deployed systems: SpAIware persistent memory poisoning via browsed web content, and a crypto-agent framework whose shared memory was manipulated to redirect transactions.
AIM (Agentic Interoperable Memory): classifies each item private (owner-only) or public (all users) and enforces index-level access control so private memories are retrievable only by their owner.
Introduces MUMBench, the first public multi-user memory benchmark covering retrieval, creation, update, and deletion across four domains.

Results over three runs: 96.0% visibility classification accuracy, 58.8% strict operation accuracy, 70.5% state-aware operation accuracy — classification is largely solved while correct multi-user operation is not.
GateMem benchmarks multi-principal shared memory (hospital, office, education, household) on utility, contextual access control, AND active forgetting after deletion.
Across baselines and backbones, no method achieves strong utility, robust access control, and reliable forgetting simultaneously.
Long-context prompting gets the best governance score at high token cost; retrieval/external-memory approaches cut cost but still leak unauthorized or deleted information.
Conclusion: current memory agents are far from reliable shared institutional deployment.

stats.fact: AIM reports 96.0% visibility classification accuracy but only 58.8% strict operation accuracy and 70.5% state-aware operation accuracy on MUMBench (3 runs), i.e. deciding private-vs-public is easier than operating correctly on a shared pool.

No current method simultaneously achieves strong utility, robust access control, and reliable forgetting for multi-principal shared memory; retrieval-based and external-memory methods still leak unauthorized or deleted information.

Four failure modes formalized for fleet memory: unauthorized leakage, stale propagation, contradiction persistence, and provenance collapse; after remediation the tested service showed 0/96 unauthorized cross-scope reads.
stats.source: arXiv:2606.24535 (Governed Shared Memory for Multi-Agent LLM Systems, Jun 2026)

stats.fact: Shared selective persistent memory reached 96% task completion vs 79% with no memory and 71% with full conversation history; retaining the right context beat retaining more (12/12 vs 8/12 trials at 3.9K vs 7.7K input tokens).
stats.source: arXiv:2607.09493 (Shared Selective Persistent Memory for Agentic LLM Systems, Jul 2026)

stats.fact: A shared memory pool creates fan-out exposure: ElizaOS researchers demonstrated a cross-user, cross-platform memory injection (Discord write hijacking an X-user transfer), confirmed only on the Sepolia testnet with no real funds lost.
stats.source: Mnemoverse, 'Shared Memory Poisoning: One Bad Write, Many Agents' (Jul 2026), citing 'Real AI Agents with Fake Memories'

stats.fact: Recalled memories compete at retrieval: in a single-agent MIMIC-III EHR setting, pre-existing legitimate memories dramatically reduced poisoning attack effectiveness (retrieval dilution).

Anthropic unified Claude chat and Claude Cowork into one account-level memory store on 25 Aug 2026: on by default for Free/Pro/Max, off by default for Team/Enterprise, sensitive topics (health, race, ethnicity, religion, politics, gender identity) excluded unless opted in, shared memory only for cloud-run Cowork, and no supported way to split the two surfaces.
stats.source: Anthropic announcement via tpsreport.news / savvymonknewsletter / TechCrunch coverage (25 Aug 2026)

stats.fact: Deleting a conversation does not delete the memory derived from it; only per-topic deletion in Settings > Memory clears it.
stats.source: Anthropic memory documentation, reported by savvymonknewsletter (Aug 2026)

stats.fact: A peer-reviewed CHI 2026 study of 20 ChatGPT users found most experienced negative expectancy violations after inspecting what the system had remembered about them, and wanted greater visibility, accessibility, transparency, and control.
stats.source: ACM CHI '26, 'Relational Gains, Privacy Strains' (10.1145/3772318.3791635, Apr 2026)

stats.fact: GDPR Article 17 (erasure), 12(3) (one-month response), 15/16 (access and rectification) and 35 (DPIA) apply directly to agent memory, while EU AI Act Article 12/19 require automatic event logging kept at least six months and Article 18 up to ten years of technical documentation — erasure versus retention.
stats.source: Codebridge, 'AI Memory Privacy and Security: A 2026 Guide' (2026)

stats.fact: Recall quality benchmarks (LongMemEval): Zep 63.8%, Mem0 49.0% — engine-level recall is a different axis from governance.
stats.source: brain.aivm.io, 'Multi-Agent Memory: One Shared Brain for AI Agents' (2026)

stats.fact: TencentDB Agent Memory 2.0 shipped team memory (Aug 3, 2026) with private-by-default assets and three visibility tiers (private / team / restricted ACLs); practitioners immediately flagged that a wrong shared memory has no correction or propagation-blocking process.
Spain's data protection authority received reports of more than 200 million personal data breaches — illustrative of how a single undifferentiated store turns one failure into a total one.
stats.source: Selina.ai, 'The Information Soup Problem' (2026), citing Contrary Research

angles: The framing shift: once memory is shared across all users, it stops being a cache and becomes multi-user infrastructure — so the load-bearing question is authorization at the storage layer, not prompt phrasing.

Derivation is the leak nobody filters: summaries, personas, and skills are new records whose ancestry no ACL follows (the PostgreSQL RLS/security_invoker precedent is the strongest analogy available).
Contextual integrity: users do not object to being remembered, they object to being surprised — 'I can't believe it stored that next to this' is an architecture finding, not a settings finding.

Fan-out poisoning: one write in a public pool is an exposure for every consumer that retrieves it, while retrieval dilution against legitimate memories is the counterweight — the honest claim is 'potential fan-out path', not 'one write compromises everyone'.
Deletion is not deletion: erasing a conversation leaves the memory it produced, and erasing a memory leaves whatever was derived from it.
Default inversion: consumer accounts get shared memory on by default while enterprise accounts get it off — a governance default that only works if the pause/reset/topic controls are visible.

Public-memory-specific risk: with all users writing one pool, there is no per-tenant boundary left to isolate, so trust must be attached to the writer (provenance + writer-trust) rather than to the space or the operator.

Practical control stack as the deliverable: write-path validation + provenance + classification, read-path storage-layer authorization with per-agent identity, lifecycle TTL/versioning, content-blind audit.
Agent-identity prerequisite: a single shared key makes per-principal permissions and a meaningful audit impossible — distinct verifiable identities come first.
Benchmark gap as the punchline: no measured method yet delivers utility + access control + forgetting together, so 'shared memory across all users' is being shipped ahead of its governance evidence.
